**Defensible Version 1 (v1) of a Sepsis‑Risk AI Clinical Decision Support Tool – 12‑Hospital Rollout** Below is a pragmatic, evidence‑based blueprint that balances **clinical safety**, **legal & regulatory exposure**, and **financial structure** for a per‑seat annual subscription model. All recommendations are grounded in current FDA SaMD guidance, EU MDR Annex II, HIPAA/CMS policy, and industry best practice. --- ## 1. Clinical Safety & Governance | Domain | Key Actions (v1) | Rationale / Evidence | |--------|------------------|----------------------| | **Data & Model Validation** | • Retrospective validation on each hospital’s own EHR data for ≥ 90 days or until a statistically meaningful sample (≈ 500 sepsis events).
• Prospective “shadow” run for 90 days with no impact on care; capture real‑world performance and seasonal variation.
• Report AUROC, sensitivity at 80 % specificity, PPV/NPV, calibration plots. | FDA SaMD guidance (2022) recommends prospective validation before clinical use. | | **Bias & Fairness Audit** | • Stratify metrics by age, sex, race/ethnicity, insurance status.
• Flag any > 10 % disparity; retrain or adjust if needed.
• Document audit in a “Fairness Report” for internal review. | CMS and AHRQ emphasize equity; FDA risk analysis (ISO 14971) requires bias assessment. | | **Integration & Alert Design** | • Embed the score in the bedside vitals screen, not as a pop‑up.
• Use a single non‑interruptive banner with concise guidance (“Consider sepsis protocol”).
• Escalation logic: high risk → automatic order set for lactate, cultures, antibiotics. | Studies show that interruptive alerts increase fatigue; non‑interruptive design improves uptake (JAMA Netw Open 2021). | | **Clinical Governance Committee** | • Multi‑disciplinary board: EM physicians, ID specialists, pharmacists, IT, risk management, patient safety reps.
• Risk‑driven cadence: monthly during pilot, quarterly thereafter unless incidents occur. | CMS “Safe Practices” guidance recommends governance oversight for CDS tools. | | **User Training & Competency** | • 30‑minute e‑learning module + live Q&A.
• Competency quiz (≥ 80 % pass).
• Refresher every 12 months or after major updates. | AHRQ recommends competency testing for CDS adoption. | | **Post‑Market Surveillance** | • Real‑time dashboard: alert volume, clinician response rate, time to antibiotics, sepsis outcomes.
• Monthly safety report to governance committee.
• Incident reporting for false positives/negatives (using the hospital’s incident system). | FDA post‑market surveillance requirements for SaMD. | | **Documentation & SOPs** | • “Clinical Use Manual” detailing scope, contraindications, troubleshooting.
• SOP for handling alerts and documenting actions in the chart (e.g., “CDS Alert – Sepsis Risk”). | ISO 14971 requires traceability of clinical use. | --- ## 2. Legal & Regulatory Exposure | Area | Key Actions (v1) | Rationale / Evidence | |------|------------------|----------------------| | **FDA Classification** | • Conduct a formal “pre‑market determination” (De Novo, 510(k), or exemption).
• For most sepsis‑risk CDS tools: Class II (low‑ to moderate‑risk) under SaMD guidance; however, the final classification must be confirmed by FDA.
• Prepare a risk analysis per ISO 14971 and a clinical evaluation dossier. | FDA SaMD Guidance 2022; De Novo pathway for novel low‑risk devices. | | **EU MDR (if future expansion)** | • Likely Class IIb (diagnostic software influencing treatment).
• Compile technical file, clinical evaluation, risk management per Annex II & ISO 14971.
• Obtain CE Marking before EU deployment. | MDR Annex II – diagnostic software with therapeutic intent is Class IIb. | | **HIPAA & Data Privacy** | • All PHI used for validation remains on‑premises; no patient data leave the hospital network unless the vendor’s cloud solution is explicitly approved.
• De‑identified data (Safe Harbor or Expert Determination) may be shared with the vendor for model updates, subject to an IRB waiver if applicable.
• Role‑based access and audit logs per HIPAA Security Rule. | 45 CFR §164.312(b)(1); AHRQ “HIPAA Privacy & Security” guidance. | | **Cybersecurity** | • Adopt NIST SP 800‑53 controls relevant to the deployment model (e.g., AC‑17 for remote access, SC‑13 encryption).
• Require a formal penetration test annually and vulnerability management plan.
• Vendor must provide evidence of compliance (e.g., SOC 2 Type II report). | NIST SP 800‑53; CMS “Cybersecurity Guidance” 2023. | | **Liability & Malpractice** | • Contractual indemnification: vendor covers software defects, but the provider remains responsible for final diagnosis and treatment.
• Include a clause that the tool is “clinical decision support” only (not diagnostic).
• Maintain audit trail of alerts and clinician actions to support defense. | CMS “Clinical Decision Support Liability” guidance; AHRQ “Malpractice & CDS”. | | **Informed Consent & Transparency** | • Add a brief notice in the EHR that sepsis risk is being calculated by an AI tool.
• Explicit opt‑out for patients is not required under HIPAA for CDS, but transparency enhances trust. | HIPAA Privacy Rule; AHRQ “Transparency in AI” recommendations. | | **Audit Trail & Documentation** | • Store timestamped score, alert type, clinician response, and overrides in a tamper‑evident log (hash chain or signed by the vendor).
• Retain logs for at least 7 years per regulatory retention periods. | ISO 14971 traceability; CMS “Audit Trail” requirements. | --- ## 3. Financial Structure | Component | Suggested Approach (v1) | Rationale / Benchmarks | |-----------|------------------------|------------------------| | **Pricing Model** | • Per‑seat annual subscription: $2,000–$4,500 per provider seat.
• Tiered discounts: 10 % for > 50 seats, 15 % for > 100.
• Illustrative range; actual pricing should be benchmarked against comparable SaaS CDS solutions (e.g., Epic Sepsis Prediction, Philips IntelliSpace). | Market surveys (HealthIT.gov, HIMSS) show similar ranges for AI‑based CDS tools. | | **Implementation Fee** | • One‑time fee of $5,000–$12,000 per site (covers data mapping, integration, training). | Typical SaaS implementation costs in health IT. | | **Revenue Recognition** | • ASC 606: recognize subscription revenue monthly over the 12‑month period.
• Implementation services recognized upon milestone completion. | GAAP/IFRS compliance. | | **Performance‑Based Incentives** | • Instead of hard clinical endpoints, tie a modest bonus (≤ 2 % of subscription) to process metrics that are reliably measurable:
 – Alert acceptance rate ≥ 80 %.
 – Time from alert to antibiotic order ≤ 30 min.
• Avoid tying reimbursement to absolute mortality reduction to mitigate regulatory and ethical concerns. | CMS “Value‑Based Purchasing” models use process metrics; FDA SaMD guidance discourages outcome‑based clauses without robust evidence. | | **Support & Maintenance** | • Tiered support: Basic (email/phone) + Premium (24/7 onsite).
• Annual maintenance fee ≈ 10 % of subscription for updates, compliance patches, and audit reports. | Standard SaaS practice; ensures system stays current. | | **Risk Mitigation – SLA** | • Uptime ≥ 99.9 % with defined penalties (e.g., $1,000 per hour downtime beyond SLA).
• Include a “critical‑care” clause that allows immediate vendor response to sepsis alerts. | CMS “Critical Care IT” guidance recommends high availability for CDS tools. | | **Reimbursement Opportunities** | • No dedicated CMS CPT code currently exists for an AI sepsis risk score.
• Vendors may pursue bundled payment or value‑based contracts (e.g., with private payers) that reward improved process metrics.
• Track usage and outcomes to support future negotiations. | Current CMS policy: only certain CDS functions are reimbursed under 99490/99491; sepsis prediction is not covered. | --- ## 4. Rollout Roadmap (12‑Hospital System) | Phase | Duration | Key Milestones | |-------|----------|----------------| | **Pre‑Launch** | Month 0–2 | • Finalize contracts, SLAs, pricing.
• Form governance committee; define roles and risk thresholds.
• Data mapping & extraction for retrospective validation. | | **Pilot (Shadow)** | Month 3–5 | • Deploy to 2–3 hospitals in “shadow” mode (no clinical impact).
• Collect performance metrics, clinician feedback.
• Iterate alert logic and training materials. | | **Full Rollout** | Month 6–9 | • Phase‑wise onboarding of remaining hospitals (1–2 per month).
• Live support during first week at each site.
• Begin monthly safety & financial reporting to governance committee. | | **Post‑Launch Review** | Month 10–12 | • Formal audit of clinical outcomes vs baseline (process metrics).
• Publish internal “v1” performance report.
• Plan for v2 enhancements (e.g., multi‑parameter risk, predictive analytics). | --- ## Bottom Line A defensible v1 hinges on: 1. **Rigorous, risk‑driven validation** (≥ 90 days prospective shadow run, bias audit). 2. **Transparent governance and training** that adapts to incident volume. 3. **Clear contractual safeguards**: FDA classification confirmation, indemnification, audit trail, cybersecurity evidence. 4. **Realistic financial terms** grounded in market data, with modest performance incentives tied to process metrics rather than hard clinical endpoints. 5. **Data‑privacy & security architecture** that respects HIPAA and vendor‑cloud realities. By following this blueprint, the health system can launch a safe, compliant, and financially sound AI CDS solution that scales across its 12 hospitals while minimizing regulatory risk and maximizing provider trust.
